title: How Crews Eat, Work & Hide Inside America's Nuclear Mountain Bunker
asof: Figures from US Air Force, Space Force & NORAD articles · sources in description

shots.s: There's a town inside this mountain.
Fifteen buildings, hidden under granite.
Every one of them sits on giant steel springs.
The front door weighs twenty-five tons.
It was built to survive a nuclear war.
So how do the people inside eat,
work,
and stay sane,
inside Cheyenne Mountain?
This is Cheyenne Mountain, outside Colorado Springs.
In the 1960s, the US blasted a complex into the rock.
It opened in 1966.
NORAD's command center was fully running by early 1967.
NORAD is run by the United States and Canada together.
So Canadian troops stand watch in here too.
The job: spot bombers and missiles heading for North America.
In the Cold War, this was the place that would sound the alarm first.
The complex covers about five acres.
On top: about eighteen hundred feet of granite.
Today it's a Space Force station.
You drive up the mountain road to a tunnel entrance.
Then you walk into the tunnel.
A long way into the rock, you reach the blast doors.
One Air Force article puts them at three and a half feet thick,
and twenty-five tons each.
Hydraulics can close them in under a minute.
Behind them: a cave with buildings inside.
Here's the strange part.
The buildings don't touch the rock.
They stand about eighteen inches from the cave walls.
And they sit on more than thirteen hundred steel springs.
Each spring weighs over a thousand pounds.
If a blast or an earthquake shakes the mountain,
the buildings bounce, instead of breaking.
Inside, crews watch the skies over North America.
Watch crews work twelve-hour shifts.
There are no windows.
One guard described working a whole shift without seeing the sun.
So the mountain has what a small town needs.
A dining facility.
A medical clinic.
Fitness centers.
A small store, a chapel, and a barber shop.
If the doors close for real, the mountain runs on its own.
Underground reservoirs are carved into the rock.
One for drinking water.
One for industrial water.
One for diesel fuel.
Together, more than four and a half million gallons.
Diesel generators can power the whole complex.
The Air Force practices this. It calls it a button-up.
Most days, nobody sleeps here.
Crews go home after their shift.
But in 2020, COVID changed that.
NORAD and Northern Command moved critical crews into the mountain.
They isolated first, then got tested,
then worked inside for weeks.
About a hundred and thirty people stood twelve-hour watches.
Between shifts, they lived apart from everyone else.
The main command center later moved to a base nearby.
But Cheyenne Mountain still stands by as the backup.
The springs are still there.
So are the twenty-five-ton doors.
Waiting for a day nobody wants.
Could you work a whole shift without seeing the sun?
